issues.legal_issue: Compensation for compulsory interference that stops an entire business is not taxable as profits of that business when no business is carried on during the period.
material_facts: The assessee carried on a business of growing tea and manufacturing tea from the leaves; the factories and premises were necessary to process the leaves into tea.
The military requisitioned the factories and related buildings while leaving the tea garden with the assessee, and the manufacture of tea stopped completely during the relevant period.
The assessee tended the tea plants, but did not carry on its tea-growing and manufacturing business during that period.

The compensation was calculated by reference to the tea that would likely have been produced, but it was paid for the injury to the business as a whole, not for the loss of a capital asset or profits of a continuing business.
issues.conclusion: The compensation was not profits of a business and was not taxable under section 10 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 10 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, tax under the head of business profits requires a business carried on by the assessee and profits produced by that business. The character of a receipt depends on what it compensates for, not the method or measure used to calculate it. Applying Income-Tax Commissioner v. Shaw Wallace & Co., income from business is the product of business activity; compensation for not carrying on a business is not such a product. The court also relied on the distinction between compensation for interruption of a continuing business and compensation where the business is stopped altogether, noting the relevant observation in Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. Newcastle Breweries, Ltd.

issues.legal_issue: Rules for apportioning receipts do not apply when compensation is not a profit of a business.
material_facts: The assessee received compensation after compulsory requisition of factories and related buildings stopped its tea manufacturing business.
No business was carried on during the relevant period, and the compensation was not a business profit.
The tax authorities had applied rules for calculating or apportioning income in assessing the compensation.
issues.conclusion: Rules 23 and 24 of the Indian Income-tax Rules, 1922, could not apply, and the compensation was not to be apportioned under those rules.
issues.legal_principle: Rules 23 and 24 of the Indian Income-tax Rules, 1922, cannot be used to calculate or apportion a receipt as business income when the receipt is not a profit of a business under section 10 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922. The conclusion that the compensation was not business profit followed from the principle in Income-Tax Commissioner v. Shaw Wallace & Co. that compensation for not carrying on business is not the product of business activity.
